opus-5.5.text:
I think for me it comes down to a pretty simple belief: technology only really changes the world when ordinary people can touch it. If you look back at personal computers, or smartphones, the real transformation didn't happen when they were powerful machines sitting in a lab or a big company. It happened when they became cheap enough, easy enough, that a student, a grandmother, a small shop owner could use them every day and find their own ways to make them useful.

Robots right now are still in that earlier stage. Most people only see them in videos, or in factories behind fences. They're expensive, they're hard to program, and you need a whole team of engineers to make them do one specific thing. So the people who get to decide what robots are for is a very small group. And I think that's a loss, because the most interesting uses usually come from people who aren't experts, who just have a problem in their own life and try something.

There's also a more practical side. A lot of the progress we've seen in AI came from data and from scale, from many people using systems and generating feedback. If robots stay rare, we simply won't collect enough real-world experience for them to get truly capable. If they become more accessible, more people use them, they encounter more situations, and the whole field improves much faster. So accessibility isn't just a nice ideal; it's actually part of how the technology matures.

And honestly, on a personal level, I just find it exciting to imagine a world where having a robot help you at home or at work feels as normal as having a phone. Not something fancy or scary, but a tool that makes life a little easier for everyone, not just for a few. That's the kind of future I'd like to help build.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making robots accessible to everyone, but does not say that his parents experiencing a robot he made would give him a greater sense of achievement.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I think about it is that a robot sitting in a lab or a factory is a very narrow thing. It solves one problem, in one place, for one group of people. But the real value of this technology only shows up when it enters ordinary life, when a family can have a robot help an elderly parent get out of bed, when a small restaurant can have one wash dishes, when someone who lives alone has something that can fold laundry and carry groceries. Those are not glamorous tasks, but they are the tasks that take up most of human life.

The second reason is more practical. In my view, robots will not become truly intelligent through a few teams working in isolation. They need to be out in the world, encountering messy kitchens, cluttered rooms, strange objects, people who behave unpredictably. That diversity of experience is the data that makes the system better. The internet made large language models possible because text was everywhere. Robots do not have that yet. The only way to get it is to put many robots into many hands and let them learn from real use. So accessibility is not only about fairness, it is also the engine of progress.

And the third reason is that I think people should have a say in what these machines become. If robots stay expensive and controlled by a few institutions, then the public only experiences them as something done to them. If they are affordable and open, people start to shape them, to find uses nobody in a lab would have imagined. That is how personal computers and smartphones developed. I would like robots to go the same way.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robots benefiting ordinary people and becoming accessible, but it does not mention Shen’s parents or say that their direct experience of a robot he made would give him a greater sense of achievement.

astra-6.text: I hope robots become more accessible because their value should reach beyond a small group of companies or researchers. They could help people with everyday tasks, take on dangerous or repetitive work, and give people more time for things they care about. Making robots easier to use and more affordable would also let more people explore what they’re useful for. Often, the people closest to a problem have the best ideas about how to solve it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses broad public access and potential uses of robots, but does not mention his parents experiencing a robot he made or the achievement that would bring him.

sol-6.1.text: I hope robots become more accessible because their value should extend beyond research labs and large companies. They could help people with everyday tasks, support older adults, and take on work that is dangerous or physically demanding. Making them more affordable and easier to use would also let more people experiment with them and discover needs that researchers might overlook. For me, the goal is to turn advances in robotics into practical benefits that more people can share.

r001.rationale: The response discusses broad public benefits of accessible robots, but does not say that Yujun’s parents experiencing a robot he made would give him a greater sense of achievement.
